questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Resistance of a filament across its working range
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the resistance of a filament changes as it heats
questions.stem: The logbook records that a small heating element reads 2.0 ohm cold and 11.0 ohm when running. Explain why the resistance of a filament changes as it heats.

answer.exemplar: The heating element is made of a metal whose resistivity rises with temperature, so as the current heats the filament its resistance increases rather than staying constant. A cold filament offers only its room-temperature resistance, and the large initial current quickly raises the temperature, after which the larger hot resistance limits the current to a steady working value. This is why a lamp often fails at switch-on, when the filament is cold and the current is largest.

questions.explanation: Metal filaments have a positive temperature coefficient, so the hotter filament resists more and the resistance climbs as it heats. That is why a cold lamp draws a large surge of current before it settles.
questions.hint: Metals get more resistant as their temperature rises.

questions.topic: The series combination relation and its precondition
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a series chain of resistors may be replaced by one resistor
questions.stem: The logbook asks why a chain of resistors in series can be treated as a single resistor at all. Explain the precondition that makes this valid.

answer.exemplar: A chain of resistors in series can be replaced by one resistor only because exactly the same current flows through every member of the chain. With a common current, the potential difference across each resistor is that current times its resistance, and these drops add along the chain, so the whole chain behaves as a single resistance equal to the sum of the members. If the current could differ between members, the drops would not add in this simple way and the replacement would fail.

questions.explanation: The chain behaves as one resistor only because the same current flows through every member, so the drops add and the resistances add. Without that shared current the replacement does not hold.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity is common to every member.

answer.exemplar: Once the charging supply is removed, the current that flows through the resistor is set by the voltage still on the capacitor, and that voltage falls as the charge is removed. answer.exemplar: A filament is a metal wire that carries the current and is heated by it, and since the resistivity of a metal rises with temperature, the resistance climbs as the filament gets hotter during use. questions.learningObjective: Calculate the current density in a heavy current-carrying lead
questions.stem: In the logbook, a welding lead of cross-section 8.0 square millimetres carries 120 A. Find the current density in units of 10^6 A per square metre.
questions.explanation: Current density is current over area, so 120 A across 8.0 x 10^-6 m^2 gives 1.5 x 10^7 A per square metre. The area must be in square metres, so convert the prefix first.
questions.hint: Divide current by the area in square metres.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The series combination relation and its precondition
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a fitted series pair is not a constant resistance
questions.stem: In the logbook, Felix fits a thermistor and a fixed resistor in series and expects the pair to behave as a single fixed resistance. Which statement identifies the problem?

options.text: The problem is that the two resistances should be subtracted rather than added.
options.misconception: suggests subtracting series resistances

options.text: The problem is that the thermistor's resistance changes with temperature, so the sum is not constant.
The problem is that the two components carry different currents in series.
options.misconception: claims series members carry different currents

options.text: The problem is that the total resistance is always less than either resistance.
options.misconception: claims the total is always the smaller value

questions.explanation: The series rule still holds, but it sums a changing thermistor resistance with a fixed one, so the pair is not constant. Series guarantees a shared current, so the fault is the varying member.
questions.hint: Series shares the current; check what changes with temperature.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The parallel combination relation and its precondition
questions.learningObjective: Explain why adding a third parallel branch changes the combined resistance
questions.stem: In the logbook, Wanjiru asks why fitting a third resistor in parallel with a pair changes the combined resistance at all. Which statement answers her?

options.text: It changes because the total current from the supply increases and so does the resistance.
options.misconception: links current increase to resistance increase

options.text: It changes because the third branch has a different voltage from the others.
options.misconception: claims parallel branches differ in voltage

options.text: It changes because the branch currents add, so the reciprocal sum grows and the combined resistance falls.
It does not change, because a parallel pair already uses the whole supply current.
options.misconception: believes adding a branch changes nothing

questions.explanation: Adding a parallel branch adds a path for current, so the currents add, the reciprocal sum grows and the combined resistance falls. The voltage stays common to every branch.
questions.hint: Adding a path lowers the combined resistance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The charging expression and what each part of it does
questions.learningObjective: Find the charge stored and the voltage needed to double it
questions.stem: In the logbook, a 470 microfarad capacitor is charged to 20.0 V. First find the charge stored in millicoulombs, then find the voltage needed to store twice that charge with the same capacitance.

options.text: Charge 9.4 mC and voltage 10.0 V, because the charge halves as the voltage doubles.
options.misconception: confuses the direction of the change

options.text: Charge 9.4 mC and voltage 40.0 V, because the charge depends on the square of the voltage.
options.misconception: gives the right numbers but the wrong law

options.text: Charge 0.0094 mC and voltage 40.0 V, because the prefix conversion is wrong.
options.misconception: misplaces the millicoulomb prefix

options.text: Charge 9.4 mC and voltage 40.0 V, because with capacitance fixed charge is proportional to voltage.

questions.explanation: Charge is Q = C V, so 470 x 10^-6 F times 20.0 V gives 0.0094 C, which is 9.4 mC. With capacitance unchanged, a doubled charge needs a doubled voltage of 40.0 V.
questions.hint: Q = C V, then double the voltage to double Q.
